item.title: Where the waiting goes
item.description:
Soundtrack · SpotifyTake Me to the Other Side · Spacemen 3The Perfect Prescription

I’ve been working on Agent Systems Lab, following some of the questions that came out of reading Donella Meadows’ Thinking in Systems. It’s a small playground for experimenting with agent workflows. This time, I wanted to look at what happens when execution gets faster while review capacity stays the same.

For me, Alfredo Artiles’ work brings together plenty of good reasons to read Meadows’ book. His Systems Thinking for Developers Workshop connects systems thinking with software development, and points back to “Martillos y clavos”, his talk at Pamplona Software Crafters in 2023. The Dev Systems Wiki contains more examples. I’d recommend these resources especially now that so many of us are building systems of agents: the feedback loops, delays and effects of changing one part of a system are things we need to understand in our own work.

The previous experiment gave me the numbers. From there, I wanted to follow a task through the system and see where it spent its time waiting. So I added a replay to the local dashboard.

For the simulation, I used 24 tasks and one simulated reviewer. A new task arrives every two ticks. Each takes eight ticks of execution and six ticks of review; these are units of model time, with no measured conversion to seconds.

I tracked each task until the reviewer made a decision on the proposed change. That includes waiting before execution and waiting after the automated work has finished.

I compared three versions:

  • A has one execution slot, so one task can execute at a time.
  • B has four execution slots, allowing up to four tasks to execute at once.
  • C has the same four slots, but at most three tasks can be between starting execution and receiving a decision.

That last rule is the work-in-progress (WIP) limit. Executing tasks, tasks waiting for review and the task being reviewed all use one of those places. A place becomes free when a decision is made. Anything waiting to start stays visible and still counts as unfinished work.

At tick 60, that limit brings the review queue down from 15 tasks in B to one in C. Both have completed eight decisions and still have 16 unfinished tasks. In C, 13 of them are waiting to start; one is executing, one is waiting for review, and one is being reviewed.

Task #11 from the saved trace makes that change easier to follow. It arrives at tick 22 in all three versions. In B, it starts straight away and then waits 44 ticks for review. In C, it waits 40 ticks before execution and four for review. Both receive a decision at tick 80.

That timing holds for every task in this particular scenario: B and C finish each task at the same tick, with the cap changing how much work has started and where it waits.

The new Experiments view brings the comparison, charts and individual task positions together. Select policy B at tick 60 and you can see the work waiting for review. Switch to C at the same tick and most of that waiting is before execution. You can go backwards through the replay to follow how each task got there, connecting the totals with the individual tasks behind them.

Play/Pause and the speed controls move through the saved trace. They affect how quickly you watch it; execution and review capacity stay the same. The dashboard guide covers local setup and how to read the different views. The scenario file contains the inputs used here.

The reviewer in this example accepts every task. There are no mistakes, requests for changes, interruptions or fatigue. A smaller review queue here says nothing about review quality or the productivity of a real team.

The next experiment will test the admission rule with actual fixture workflows: whether a task waiting for a human decision keeps its place, including after a restart. That behavior still needs implementing and testing.

item.title: A clearer view of agent activity
item.description:
Soundtrack · SpotifyMediation · OvalSystemisch

I’ve updated the dashboard in Agent Systems Lab. I wanted to make it easier to follow what each agent has done, where tasks are waiting and how long they have been there.

The agents shown here work on tasks with a limited set of tools. The dashboard shows which tools each role can use and how to intervene through the operator’s terminal. It also lets me compare the recorded history with a saved checkpoint.

Two different kinds of waiting

The dashboard shows two queues separately. One is work waiting for human review: a task needs someone to make a decision. The other is records waiting to be sent: an observation still needs to reach its receiver. Keeping them separate helps me see what needs attention.

A reference point for history

A saved checkpoint gives me a reference for checking the history. It contains an event count and a digital fingerprint of the history up to that point. I can compare that reference with the recorded history later, even after more events have been added.

That check tells me whether the earlier history still matches. It doesn’t encrypt the records or prevent a database administrator from rewriting them. To detect changes against a checkpoint I trust, I need to keep that copy separately.

The illustrated dashboard guide goes through each view with annotated screenshots and examples. It’s written for developers who already use AI assistants and are getting started with agent systems.

This is still an experimental playground. The examples use scripted model responses and test records to show how the workflow and controls behave. They don’t establish the quality of real models or tell us whether workers are healthy.

item.title: Agent Systems Lab: when review becomes the bottleneck
item.description:
Soundtrack · SpotifyFaces and Names · Lou Reed & John CaleSongs For Drella

The conversations I’ve been having about agentic systems took me back to Donella Meadows’ Thinking in Systems. I wanted to explore one of those questions about feedback loops, delays and bottlenecks: what happens when we can execute more work, but our capacity to review it stays the same?

To try it, I used a small, deterministic model in Agent Systems Lab. It lets me change one rule at a time and keep track of every task that is still waiting.

What I put in the model

The model follows tasks through execution and review. A task can wait before it starts executing, then wait again once it is ready for review. I count both queues, along with the tasks executing, being reviewed and already decided.

The reviewer is a simulated resource. It is separate from the playground’s Reviewer agent: this experiment does not run the Researcher, Builder or Reviewer agents, call a model provider, or involve a human reviewer. Time advances in logical ticks, with no measured conversion to seconds.

The checked-in scenario has 24 tasks arriving every two ticks, from tick 0 to tick 46. Each takes eight ticks to execute and six to review. There is one reviewer, and every review accepts.

I kept that workload fixed and compared three versions:

  • A has one execution slot and no work-in-progress limit.
  • B has four execution slots and no work-in-progress limit.
  • C has the same four slots, but at most three tasks can be between starting execution and receiving a decision.

That work-in-progress (WIP) limit includes tasks executing, waiting for review and being reviewed. Each decision frees a place for another task to start. Tasks waiting to start are outside the limit, but I still count them as unfinished. Otherwise, I could make the system look better just by leaving some of its waiting out of the report.

Moving from A to B changes execution capacity. Moving from B to C changes only the admission limit, which controls when a task can start. The arrivals and the time each task needs for execution and review stay the same.

Where the tasks are waiting

I first looked at tick 60, after processing all the transitions at that tick:

Tasks at tick 60 A B C
Decisions completed 6 8 8
Total unfinished 18 16 16
Waiting for admission 16 0 13
Executing 1 0 1
Waiting for review 0 15 1
Being reviewed 1 1 1

With four execution slots, B has completed eight decisions. With one slot, A has completed six. That is four times the execution capacity and 8/6, or about 1.33 times, as many decisions during this window. B has also built up a queue of 15 tasks waiting for review.

The reviewer has stayed the same while more work has become ready for it. The exact ratio depends on startup and on where I stop to look, so I wouldn’t use 1.33 as a rule for how agent systems scale.

C has completed the same eight decisions as B, with only one task waiting for review. But 13 tasks are now waiting to start. Both versions still have 16 unfinished tasks.

The cap changes where the waiting happens; demand and review capacity stay the same. I also followed all 24 tasks through to their final decision to check whether the result was just an effect of stopping at tick 60:

Full workload, logical ticks A B C
Final decision 198 152 152
End-to-end time, p50 / p95 80 / 146 58 / 102 58 / 102
Admission wait, p50 / p95 66 / 132 0 / 0 40 / 84
Review-queue wait, p50 / p95 0 / 0 44 / 88 4 / 4

Each task receives its decision at the same tick in B as it does in C. C starts less work at once and still keeps the reviewer supplied. The time saved in the review queue is spent waiting before execution instead.

The p50 and p95 values use the nearest-rank method and cover all 24 tasks in each version. At tick 60, only six tasks have finished in A and eight in B and C. Comparing the times of only those completed tasks would mean comparing different groups, so I’ve kept the full-workload timings together.

Running the experiment

When I prepared this article, I reran the scenario and compared it with the published reference. Both the scenario hash and the deterministic report hash matched. The source links and commands here refer to public revision 8bf1669a68a9072326d35abfb18ee979a3766531.

You’ll need Git, uv and Python 3.11 or newer:

git clone https://github.com/saski/agent-systems-lab.git
cd agent-systems-lab
git checkout 8bf1669a68a9072326d35abfb18ee979a3766531
make setup
uv run --locked systems-lab experiment review-capacity \
  --scenario experiments/review-capacity/scenario.json

The command prints a manifest pointing to a new directory under .lab/experiments/review-capacity/. In it, you can inspect scenario.json, report.json and manifest.json. The expected deterministic report SHA-256 is:

a3a9c0396620438fa7c039f5aa9aace98a85cff968ba5004c52e5e25f473e58a

You can run this numerical experiment without Docker. The command invokes no model providers or agent workers. The experiment guide includes charts, metric definitions and a replay of the saved trace that you can open locally. On GitHub, that HTML guide appears as source; the replay does not run there.

What I’d measure in a real workflow

I’d measure arrivals, waiting before execution, execution itself, waiting for review and accepted output together. If I only looked at execution speed or the length of the review queue, I would miss some of the time tasks spend in the system.

The WIP limit is something I would test in that workflow. Here it bounds admitted work without slowing down delivery compared with B. Whether that helps in practice depends on things this model leaves out, such as stale context, interruptions, deadlines and work that needs another pass.

The workload here is finite and scheduled, every task takes the same amount of execution and review time, and every review accepts. There is no randomness, rework, fatigue, failure or measure of quality. I can use it to follow what happens to unfinished work when execution capacity grows and review stays fixed. It cannot tell me a real reviewer’s capacity, the best WIP limit, whether agents are safe, or whether a team would become more productive.

The revision used here includes the numerical model and CLI, with a standalone learning guide as documentation. It predates the integrated Experiments dashboard. I’ve since added that view; Where the waiting goes follows the same experiment through its replay and shows the timelines.

You can inspect the simulation and metric calculations, or read how I organise the surrounding tools in Arnesto.

item.title: Arnesto: cómo organizo mi entorno de agentes
item.description:
Soundtrack · SpotifyMoyege - Mark's Disco Dub · Mark ErnestusLagos Shake: A Tony Allen Chop Up

Arnesto es el entorno que uso para trabajar con agentes. Ahí junto las reglas, los skills, el contexto y las herramientas, con unas cuantas decisiones sobre qué puede hacer cada una. Lo publico para quien quiera mirar dentro o construir su propio arnés. Incluye mis necesidades, mis manías y mis puñetas, así que no espero que alguien lo instale entero y le encaje tal cual.

Empezó en el Q3 de 2025 como un fork de la configuración de Eduardo Ferro Aldama. Durante bastante tiempo se llamó Augmented Code Configuration, hasta que aquello fue creciendo más allá de las reglas para una herramienta de coding y el nombre se quedó corto. Arnesto salió de juntar arnés con Ernesto.

Para explicar cómo lo organizo, voy a recorrer algunas de esas decisiones con enlaces a los archivos donde están recogidas. Los ejemplos corresponden a la versión pública del 6 de octubre de 2026.

Qué cargo en cada tarea

Hay unas pocas instrucciones que quiero mantener presentes en cualquier tarea: entender el objetivo antes de tocar nada, hacer el cambio más pequeño que resuelva el problema, verificarlo y explicar lo que queda incierto. Están en .agents/rules/base.md.

El detalle de Python, React o Makefile lo cargo cuando hace falta, y las convenciones de cada repositorio se quedan en ese repositorio. Así evito que una instrucción pensada para un proyecto condicione el trabajo en los demás. «No digas que una comprobación ha pasado si no la has ejecutado» me sirve siempre; las instrucciones de un pipeline de BigQuery, cuando estoy trabajando con BigQuery.

Con los skills sigo la misma idea. Un skill recoge un procedimiento que puedo reutilizar, por ejemplo para revisar un Dockerfile, preparar una entrevista o trabajar con un documento. Busco el que encaja con la tarea y abro su SKILL.md.

Para encontrarlo uso primero el catálogo del cliente con el que estoy trabajando. Si no tiene uno, consulto la sección correspondiente del catálogo por dominio. El inventario completo me sirve para mantener la biblioteca, pero cargarlo al principio de cada tarea añade información que no necesito en ese momento.

Que dos herramientas puedan leer el mismo procedimiento tampoco les da acceso a lo mismo. Compartir un skill no comparte la sesión del navegador, las credenciales ni los permisos de la otra herramienta.

Cómo continúo una tarea entre sesiones

En una tarea larga necesito poder recuperar por qué tomé una decisión sin volver a reconstruir toda la conversación. Planning e intentional compaction me ayudaron a conservar lo importante; aquí debo mucho a HumanLayer y Dexter Horthy. OpenSpec añadió una estructura para conectar requisitos, decisiones, ejecución y verificación, gracias también a Alvaro Moya.

En Arnesto guardo las especificaciones en docs/openspec/, y la investigación y los planes en thoughts/. Son archivos a los que puedo volver cuando continúo el trabajo en otra sesión.

Las recetas y la evidencia de un experimento, en cambio, se quedan en el proyecto que lo realiza. Los logs completos y el estado temporal quedan fuera del historial publicado. En Arnesto conservo los mecanismos que puedo reutilizar para coordinar ese trabajo; la guía de artefactos de coordinación explica qué va en cada sitio.

Qué comparto entre herramientas

Trabajo con Codex, Cursor, Claude o Gemini en local; con Hermes a través de Telegram; y con OpenCode y OmniRoute en algunas rutas de ejecución. También voy evaluando otras herramientas. Quiero poder cambiar esas piezas y conservar las convenciones que ya me funcionan.

Para conectar las reglas y los skills con los clientes compatibles uso setup-symlinks.sh. Algunas configuraciones se inicializan desde templates/ y después se mantienen en el entorno de la propia herramienta. No todas las configuraciones son enlaces vivos al repositorio.

Las credenciales, las sesiones, las bases de datos locales y los permisos siguen siendo responsabilidad de cada herramienta. Por eso mantengo separados los directorios de Codex y Orca: contienen bastante más que una preferencia de modelo. Esa decisión está documentada en la guía de límites entre runtimes.

Cuando delego una tarea

El adaptador de workers es un ejemplo de cómo acoto el trabajo que delego. Su contrato declara el directorio de trabajo, los archivos permitidos, la sensibilidad del material, el modelo y la validación. Este fragmento muestra parte de esa estructura:

{
  "task_class": "bounded_code",
  "sensitivity": "non_sensitive",
  "allowed_files": ["README.md"],
  "validation": {
    "command": ["make", "test"]
  },
  "require_changes": true
}

El fragmento sirve para explicar el formato; no es un contrato completo con el que lanzar un worker. En este adaptador, allowed_files comprueba qué archivos han cambiado después de la ejecución. No impide que el proceso escriba en otros sitios. El adaptador tampoco aísla la red ni el sistema de archivos, así que esa lista en el JSON no permite afirmar que el proceso esté aislado.

Delegar deja en manos de quien coordina la preparación del alcance, la revisión del diff y la ejecución de las comprobaciones. Si alguna no se ha ejecutado, el resultado debe decirlo. Si el trabajo se envía a un proveedor externo, el material tiene que estar autorizado para ese destino.

Por dónde empezaría

Para montar un entorno propio empezaría por una regla que evite un fallo recurrente, un skill para una tarea habitual y un lugar donde conservar requisitos y decisiones. Después probaría esas piezas con trabajo real. Copiar todos mis modelos, rutas y clientes de golpe haría difícil saber qué aporta cada uno.

La guía de desarrollo y el Makefile permiten ver cómo compruebo la configuración del repositorio. Esas comprobaciones detectan incoherencias concretas. Que pasen no demuestra que cualquier agente vaya a comportarse bien en cualquier tarea.

Mientras sigo cambiando herramientas, quiero poder explicar las decisiones que he tomado, ver dónde están los límites y revisar lo que ha ocurrido con suficiente evidencia. Para explorar qué pasa cuando muchas tareas llegan a la revisión humana, estoy usando Agent Systems Lab.

item.title: Using AI without outsourcing the learning
item.description:
Anthropic published research on AI assistance and coding skills that made me think about what we learn while getting work done.

In a randomized study, 52 mostly junior software engineers with Python experience worked with Trio, an unfamiliar asynchronous programming library. Some had access to an AI assistant; others worked without it.

Three findings stood out:

  • Learning: the AI group averaged 50% on the subsequent assessment, compared with 67% in the control group. That is a gap of 17 percentage points.
  • Speed: the AI group finished about two minutes faster on average, but the difference was not statistically significant.
  • Debugging: this was the area with the largest gap, which matters when the next task is to inspect and supervise generated code.

The researchers also looked at how participants used the assistant. Asking for explanations and building understanding were associated with better learning outcomes than delegating the work wholesale. Those interaction patterns came from small groups; they are useful signals, not proof that a particular prompting style causes better learning.

My takeaway is to treat AI as a comprehension partner when learning something new: ask why, inspect the result, and make sure I can explain and debug it myself. Finishing a task and understanding it are different outcomes, and I want to keep paying attention to both.

This study concerns a specific learning task and an immediate assessment. It does not establish what happens to long-term expertise or to experienced developers working in familiar codebases.

item.title: From execution to coordination: product and engineering
item.description:
Over the last few months, much of the AI tooling I have been following in software has targeted code execution: tests, bugs, docs, security. Automating the technical lower layers. The new wave of agentic tools shifts towards finished knowledge work: analysis, reporting, planning, and all with minimal supervision. That’s automation moving from execution into coordination.

If you abstract the PM role, much of it is cognitive orchestration: understanding context, synthesizing inputs, defining problems, prioritizing, specifying intent, aligning stakeholders, validating outcomes. These are exactly the structured knowledge workflows agents are starting to absorb. So yes, parts of the Product domain are now in scope for automation, just like parts of engineering were until now.

The shift I see in engineering is toward system design, orchestration and problem framing. That is where I expect more of our value to sit as implementation becomes easier.

A similar shift is reaching product. What remains is the PM as a decision architect inside increasingly automated socio-technical systems. Which is also why product and engineering are converging: engineers move toward product definition as implementation friction drops, while PMs move toward system design as coordination becomes programmable.

Rich Holmes’ example of a product workflow using Claude Cowork prompted this reflection.

Here is another flow from the same source: Rich Holmes’ example with the Ideate Agent in Stitch

item.title: Equipos donde las personas crecen y quieren quedarse
item.description:
¡Hola, vengo a dar las gracias!

Me emociona recibir el Make It Happen Spirit Award de Eventbrite tras una etapa de casi ocho años en Eventbrite en los que he tenido la suerte de crecer, equivocarme, aprender y asumir (¡muy!) distintos tipos de responsabilidad, pasando de Staff Engineer a Engineering Manager.

Esto no se habría logrado sin el talento, la empatía, la visión, la generosidad y la confianza de la gente con la que he trabajado durante todo este tiempo (¡hola, Juan Iglesias!). Equipos que se implican, que se cuidan, que discuten con rigor y que empujan juntos cuando las cosas se ponen difíciles. Este premio es, sobre todo, suyo.

Me emociona especialmente que se reconozca no solo el impacto técnico y los resultados, sino también una forma de hacer: conectar decisiones de ingeniería con valor real para clientes, construir sistemas sólidos y, al mismo tiempo, crear espacios donde las personas crecen y quieren quedarse.

Gracias a todas las personas que me han acompañado en este camino. Y a todos los que os habéis alegrado de forma genuina ✨

Seguimos.

item.title: Less magic, more discipline: working with context
item.description:
I've been following Eduardo Ferro Aldama's explorations about augmented coding Cursor commands added to augmentedcode-configuration

Those sent me down a deeper path: how to reduce AI hallucinations and keep coding sessions genuinely productive, not just fast. One piece that really clicked was “Tu CLAUDE.md no funciona (sin Context Engineering)”: Tu CLAUDE.md no funciona (sin Context Engineering)

From there, I got to the Frequent Intentional Compaction (FIC) framework, and this implementation as a Claude plugin: stepwise-dev

So, I decided to get my hands dirty and cloned Edu’s augmented coding tools repo: my augmentedcode-configuration fork …adding a translation of the FIC Claude plugin, wiring it up as Cursor commands.

Still experimenting, but chasing the idea of explicit, repeated compaction of intent and context feels like gaining control when using these tools for coding. Less magic, more discipline.
